title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1, preregistration SHA-256 archived) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc inferential sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is a central NetOps task. Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can synthesize configuration templates from high‑level intent but also exhibits failure modes (omission, misordering, unsafe commands) that threaten operational safety. Community recommendations increasingly favor guarded architectures that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators and bounded repair loops (generate→verify→repair) to provide a floor‑safety net. However, rigorous preregistered evaluations that quantify the incremental effect of tightly bounded validator+repair pipelines on first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics are scarce. We executed a preregistered paired experiment to measure whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single shared candidate generation by an LLM (declared model: gpt-5-mini), a frozen deterministic validator, and at most one automated repair attempt—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration compared with using the single shared candidate alone. The study is narrowly scoped to this estimand and to the preregistered sampling semantics to provide reproducible, artifact‑grounded evidence and methodological guidance for future NetOps confirmatory work.
sections.related_work: LLM applications to intent‑driven configuration and NetOps have rapidly expanded; system demonstrations and lab evaluations show promising synthesis capabilities but also highlight operational risks such as hallucinations and ordering errors [10.1002/nem.2313]. Adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair) provide empirical evidence that verifier‑assisted pipelines and deterministic safety nets reduce factual errors and improve grounding, supporting the guarded architecture for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Foundational network verification work (e.g., header‑space and specification‑based checking) offers algorithmic primitives for deterministic validators that statically reason about reachability and policy constraints [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Surveys and evaluation proposals emphasize the need for generate→verify→repair benchmarks and auditability in agentic NetOps workflows [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our study situates itself at this intersection by executing a preregistered paired test that isolates the incremental effect of a validator plus a single automated repair iteration on acceptance of an LLM‑produced configuration.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The study was preregistered as cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 before observing outcomes; the preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest. Confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration included an explicit planning assumption (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) used for power calculations; because this assumption directly affects interpretability of H1, it is reported here in Methods to make clear that the confirmatory design depended on that baseline prevalence.

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with 300 deterministic seeds produced by a frozen task generator (task IDs 0001–0300). The experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each seed the generator produced one single candidate configuration that served as the baseline response and the starting point for guarded validation and possible repair. This preregistered pairing emulates an operational workflow where a single plan is reviewed and remediated. Planned episodes = 600 (baseline + guarded per seed). Initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The shared‑candidate pairing raises within‑pair correlation and consequently reduces expected discordant pairs available to paired inference relative to independent draws; we explicitly accounted for this tradeoff in the preregistration and in the power plan.

Model and sampling determinism: The declared generation model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. The execution/model_configuration.json (sha256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa) records declared_model_version: "gpt-5-mini" and shows temperature = null (unset). Because the temperature field was not explicitly set in the archived model configuration, sampling determinism is not specified by the artifacts: the manifest records temperature=null rather than an explicit deterministic seed or zero temperature. We therefore state explicitly that sampling determinism is unspecified in the recorded execution artifacts and discuss inferential implications below (see Limitations and Disclosure). The provider default sampling behavior (if any) is not asserted beyond the archived model_configuration.json.

Validator, canonicalization, and scoring semantics: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalizes generated text into a normalized configuration AST and applies static checks derived from task‑level workflow policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, minimum_active_in_groups). Success is defined by full intent‑constraint validation: the canonicalized configuration must satisfy the task's required_sequence and expected_final_state and trigger no validator violations. Validator traces include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid flag; these traces are the operational inputs to repair invocation and scoring.

Repair adapter and budget: The preregistered repair adapter is invoked only when the validator reports violations on the shared candidate. The adapter is restricted to a single automated repair attempt per episode and is designed to perform minimal targeted edits to remove reported violations while preserving the original plan where allowed. Repair prompts and repair responses were archived; repair outcomes were revalidated by the same deterministic validator to produce the final guarded decision.

Contamination and exclusions: The preregistration specified deterministic contamination checks (normalized‑AST exact equality and near‑duplicate thresholds) and deterministic replacement rules from a preregistered reserve list if exact duplicates were found. The execution manifest records no contamination exclusions for the analyzed set; all such checks and any replacements would be logged in the manifest.

Primary estimand and analysis plan: The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference). The preregistered primary test is the exact McNemar two‑sided test at α=0.05; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute paired difference were preregistered with 10,000 resamples and explicit seed (seed = 1729). Secondary analyses included conditional repair success CIs and stratified checks. The analysis executor and artifacts are archived and are the authoritative source for the counts and intervals reported below.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared initial generation calls + 1 repair invocation). No provider/infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy. Per‑task normalized responses, validator decisions, and repair traces are archived and are the direct source of the numerical counts below (see execution manifest and analysis artifacts referenced in the Disclosure Statement).

Primary outcomes (archived counts): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency derived from the archived paired_contingency_table.csv (sha256 = 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. These contingency counts are the direct inputs to the preregistered McNemar test and bootstrap CI.

Inferential results (preregistered): Exact McNemar two‑sided test on the observed contingency gives p = 1.00. Observed absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = (n10 − n01)/N = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap seed = 1729; bootstrap artifact is archived). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for 1/1 is [0.025, 1.0]. All numeric outputs above are reproducible from the archived analysis artifacts referenced in the execution manifest.

Why p = 1.00 for the observed contingency: the exact McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant total (n10 + n01 = 1). With only one discordant pair, the conditional test distribution admits only symmetric outcomes that render a two‑sided exact p non‑small; consequently the test returns p = 1.00 for this observed pattern. The paired bootstrap CI (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) provides complementary interval information showing the same practical limitation: the observed data are consistent only with extremely small absolute improvements given the single discordant pair. Both the paired_contingency_table.csv (sha256 noted above) and the archived bootstrap outputs reproduce these numerical facts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation tied to archived artifacts. The archived contingency (n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0) imposes a strict limit on resolvable paired effects: absolute paired difference = (n10 − n01)/N, so with N=300 the maximal observed absolute improvement equals 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. The preregistered planning arithmetic assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40 and targeted a ≥50% relative reduction in fail rate; that target corresponds to an absolute increase in pass rate ≈ 0.30 and would require on the order of 90 net discordant pairs favoring the guarded arm for N=300. The empirical near‑ceiling baseline therefore eliminated the statistical headroom envisioned in the preregistration; this artifact‑grounded explanation is documented in the execution and analysis artifacts and motivates explicit design choices for future studies.

Pairing semantics and power tradeoffs. The shared_initial_candidate design intentionally models remediation of a single generated plan and increases ecological validity for operational remediation use cases, but it also reduces expected discordant counts and therefore paired test power. Researchers must match pairing semantics to the operational estimand and translate that match into power calculations: i.e., when using shared candidates, one must either calibrate task difficulty to increase baseline failure prevalence or increase N to reach the desired discordant counts for a target absolute effect. The deterministic task difficulty fields and the contingency artifacts archived in the execution bundle enable precise arithmetic for such planning.

Repair as a conditional estimand. H2 (repair effectiveness) is conditional on initial failures. The observed repair result (1/1 corrected) demonstrates feasibility but is statistically imprecise (CI wide). If repair effectiveness is the primary operational claim, preregistrations should plan for an expected number of initial failures (for example via adversarial augmentation or increased task difficulty) so that conditional repair success can be estimated with required precision.

Construct validity and emulation. Our validator performs deterministic static checks and canonicalization without executing configurations in devices or emulators. This design improves safety (no live changes) but limits construct validity for runtime properties (control‑plane convergence, transient reachability). If claims about runtime consequences are intended, future studies should integrate emulation/simulation stages with preregistered mappings from dynamic emulator outcomes to success/failure. The execution manifest explicitly records that validation was static and that dynamic emulation was not used.

Operational implications. A frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded repair loop can correct at least some invalid LLM candidates without human intervention—the single observed correction is an example—but whether such pipelines materially reduce first‑pass misconfiguration in production depends critically on baseline error prevalence and validator coverage. When baseline errors are rare, the primary operational value of the guarded pipeline may be catastrophic‑risk prevention rather than throughput gains. Organizations should align evaluation design (task bank difficulty, pairing semantics, emulation inclusion) with their operational acceptance and governance thresholds.

Reproducibility and diagnostics. The value of structured deterministic validator traces is clear: normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and repair_applied flags enable interpretable failure‑mode analysis and reproducible post‑mortems. The execution manifest enumerates these per‑task artifacts and is the authoritative source for the counts and traces cited above.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) to measure the incremental effect of a frozen deterministic validator plus a single automated repair iteration on LLM‑generated network configurations (declared model: gpt-5-mini). Observed artifact counts show baseline 299/300 valid and guarded 300/300 valid; the single automated repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output. However, the observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40), eliminating statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target and rendering H1 effectively not testable as originally posed. The run highlights concrete methodological lessons: preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets, calibrate task difficulty (or adversarially augment) to ensure sufficient initial failures or discordant pairs for planned effect sizes, and include emulation when runtime semantics matter. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic static configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

Model configuration recorded temperature = null (unset) in execution/model_configuration.json (sha256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa); because sampling determinism is not specified in the archived artifact, we cannot assert deterministic generation behavior and this increases uncertainty about sampling variability in repeated runs.

H2 (repair‑success) evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
